newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: Mandela's ANC ponders naming its apartheid spies.
newsitem.headline: Mandela's ANC ponders naming its apartheid spies.

text.p: South Africa's ruling African National Congress (ANC) met in Johannesburg on Monday to decide whether to reveal the names of alleged apartheid-era informers now in President Nelson Mandela's government.

A lawyer representing former policemen and a self-confessed apartheid-era assassin have alleged that up to five ANC cabinet ministers spied on their own colleagues on behalf of the white government during the war over apartheid.
ANC spokesman Ronnie Mamoepa said the meeting of the ANC's national working committee would be headed by Deputy President Thabo Mbeki and ANC acting secretary-general Cheryl Carolus.

"We have noted that the issue of former state security informers has attracted a great deal of attention, including that of former apartheid disinformation networks, some of whom have now begun to disseminate deceit and lies against carefully selected leading members of the ANC.
"The committee will deliberate upon the matter and a full statement will be released thereafter," Mamoepa said.
The outcome will be a test for the ANC, which has promoted open government and transparency in politics since it swept to power in the country's first all-race elections in 1994.
The allegations surfaced during enquiries by the statutory Truth and Reconciliation Commission (TRC) headed by Archbishop Desmond Tutu.
Roelof du Plessis, a lawyer representing five apartheid agents seeking amnesty, told the TRC there were high profile people in government who were informers.
Joe Mamasela, who has confessed to several political murders, said five ANC cabinet ministers had once worked for the apartheid police.
The TRC's amnesty committee initially ruled that spies identified during applications for immunity from prosecution for human rights crimes would not be publicly named.
But Tutu said last week it would be necessary to name the people implicated after giving them 21 days' advance notice in order to halt the spread of lies and innuendo.
Mbeki and Mandela have come out in favour of naming the alleged informers, with Mandela saying anyone whose actions led to deaths would be fired from the cabinet.

Mandela said during his four-nation tour of southeast Asia last week that intelligence reports showed there were "high profile people, not necessarily in cabinet," who had informed on their colleagues in the past.

Scores of police and soldiers who served the white governments of the past have given testimony to Tutu's commission or the amnesty committee about torture, kidnapping and assassination aimed at the ANC.
But ANC members accused of human rights abuses in the movement's training camps have yet to appear before the TRC.
"We have no interest in protecting informers," Matthews Phosa, the ANC's legal adviser and now premier of Mpumalanga province told state radio on Monday.
The TRC, set up to heal apartheid's wounds, can grant indemnity from prosecution to those who confess to crimes or human rights abuses committed on either side of the race war.
